statement: To construct a pyramid, to comprehend it in a given sphere, and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid.
heath_proof: Let the diameter AB of the given sphere be set out, and let it be cut at the point C so that AC is double of CB; let the semicircle ADB be described on AB, let CD be drawn from the point C at right angles to AB, and let DA be joined; let the circle EFG which has its radius equal to DC be set out, let the equilateral triangle EFG be inscribed in the circle EFG, [IV. 2] let the centre of the circle, the point H, be taken, [III. 1] let EH, HF, HG be joined; from the point H let HK be set up at right angles to the plane of the circle EFG, [XI. 12] let HK equal to the straight line AC be cut off from HK, and let KE, KF, KG be joined. Now, since KH is at right angles to the plane of the circle EFG, therefore it will also make right angles with all the straight lines which meet it and are in the plane of the circle EFG. [XI. Def. 3] But each of the straight lines HE, HF, HG meets it: therefore HK is at right angles to each of the straight lines HE, HF, HG. And, since AC is equal to HK, and CD to HE, and they contain right angles, therefore the base DA is equal to the base KE. [I. 4] For the same reason each of the straight lines KF, KG is also equal to DA; therefore the three straight lines KE, KF, KG are equal to one another. And, since AC is double of CB, therefore AB is triple of BC. But, as AB is to BC, so is the square on AD to the square on DC, as will be proved afterwards. Therefore the square on AD is triple of the square on DC. But the square on FE is also triple of the square on EH, [XIII. 12] and DC is equal to EH; therefore DA is also equal to EF. But DA was proved equal to each of the straight lines KE, KF, KG; therefore each of the straight lines EF, FG, GE is also equal to each of the straight lines KE, KF, KG; therefore the four triangles EFG, KEF, KFG, KEG are equilateral. Therefore a pyramid has been constructed out of four equilateral triangles, the triangle EFG being its base and the point K its vertex. It is next required to comprehend it in the given sphere and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid. For let the straight line HL be produced in a straight line with KH, and let HL be made equal to CB. Now, since, as AC is to CD, so is CD to CB, [VI. 8] while AC is equal to KH, CD to HE, and CB to HL, therefore, as KH is to HE, so is EH to HL; therefore the rectangle KH, HL is equal to the square on EH. [VI. 17] And each of the angles KHE. EHL is right; therefore the semicircle described on KL will pass through E also. [cf. VI. 8, III. 31.] If then, KL remaining fixed, the semicircle be carried round and restored to the same position from which it began to be moved, it will also pass through the points F, G, since, if FL, LG be joined, the angles at F, G similarly become right angles; and the pyramid will be comprehended in the given sphere. For KL, the diameter of the sphere, is equal to the diameter AB of the given sphere, inasmuch as KH was made equal to AC, and HL to CB. I say next that the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid For, since AC is double of CB, therefore AB is triple of BC; and, convertendo, BA is one and a half times AC. But, as BA is to AC, so is the square on BA to the square on AD. Therefore the square on BA is also one and a half times the square on AD. And BA is the diameter of the given sphere, and AD is equal to the side of the pyramid. Therefore the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid.

13.13
**Statement:** To construct a pyramid, to comprehend it in a given sphere, and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a diameter of the given sphere (D11.17). Cut off from AB its third part CB (6.9); then AC is double of CB, and AB, being AC together with CB, is triple of CB (CN2).

**Step 2.** Bisect AB at O (1.10), and with centre O and distance OA describe the semicircle ADB on AB (P3). From the point C draw CD at right angles to AB (1.11), meeting the circumference at D, and join DA, DB (P1).

**Step 3.** The angle ADB is an angle in a semicircle, so it is right (3.31). In the right-angled triangle ADB the perpendicular DC has been drawn from the right angle to the base AB; hence the triangles ADC, DBC are similar to the whole triangle ADB and to one another (6.8), and the sides about their equal angles are proportional (6.4): BA : AD = AD : AC, and AC : CD = CD : CB. Therefore the square on AD is equal to the rectangle BA, AC, and the square on CD is equal to the rectangle AC, CB (6.17).

**Step 4.** The rectangles BA, AC and AC, CB stand under the same height AC, so they are to one another as their bases (6.1): rectangle BA, AC : rectangle AC, CB = BA : CB. Hence, by Step 3, the square on AD : the square on CD = AB : CB. But AB is triple of CB (Step 1); therefore the square on AD is triple of the square on CD.

**Step 5.** Take a point H in any plane, and with centre H and distance equal to CD describe the circle EFG (P3). Construct an equilateral triangle (1.1); its three angles are equal to one another (1.5). In the circle EFG inscribe a triangle EFG equiangular with it (4.2); having its three angles equal, it has its three sides equal (1.6), so EFG is an equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle. Join HE, HF, HG (P1). These are radii of the circle, so HE = HF = HG = CD (D1.15).

**Step 6.** Since the equilateral triangle EFG is inscribed in the circle whose radius is HE, the square on EF is triple of the square on EH (13.12), that is, triple of the square on CD. But the square on AD is also triple of the square on CD (Step 4). Therefore the square on AD is equal to the square on EF (CN1), and AD = EF.

**Step 7.** From H set up HK at right angles to the plane of the circle EFG (11.12), cut off HK equal to AC (1.3), and join KE, KF, KG (P1). Since KH is at right angles to the plane, it makes right angles with HE, HF, HG, which meet it and lie in that plane (D11.3): the angles KHE, KHF, KHG are right.

**Step 8.** In the triangles KHE, ACD the two sides KH, HE are equal to the two sides AC, CD respectively, and the included angles KHE, ACD are equal, both being right (P4); therefore the base KE is equal to the base AD (1.4). In the same way KF = AD and KG = AD. Hence KE = KF = KG = AD = EF = FG = GE (CN1, Step 6). Thus the solid figure constructed from the base EFG to the point K, which is a pyramid (D11.12), is contained by the four equilateral triangles EFG, KEF, KFG, KGE. A pyramid has been constructed.

**Step 9.** Produce KH beyond H to L (P2), cut off HL equal to CB (1.3), and bisect KL at M (1.10). Then KL, being KH together with HL, is equal to AC together with CB, that is, to AB (CN2).

**Step 10.** Since KH = AC, HL = CB and HE = CD, the rectangle KH, HL is equal to the rectangle AC, CB, which is equal to the square on CD (Step 3); hence the rectangle KH, HL is equal to the square on HE.

**Step 11.** The straight line KL is cut into equal segments at M and into unequal segments at H; therefore the rectangle KH, HL together with the square on HM is equal to the square on KM (2.5). By Step 10, the square on HE together with the square on HM is equal to the square on KM.

**Step 12.** Since the angle KHE is right (Step 7), the adjacent angle EHL is also right (1.13); so HE is at right angles to the whole line KL, and, M lying on KL, the angle EHM is right. Join EM (P1). In the right-angled triangle EHM the square on EM is equal to the squares on EH, HM (1.47), which together are equal to the square on KM (Step 11). Therefore EM = KM.

**Step 13.** Join FM, GM (P1). In the triangles EHM, FHM the two sides EH, HM are equal to the two sides FH, HM (Step 5), and the included angles EHM, FHM are right and therefore equal (P4); so FM = EM (1.4). Likewise GM = EM. Hence MK, ML, ME, MF, MG are all equal to one another (CN1).

**Step 14.** With centre M and distance MK describe a semicircle on KL (P3), and let it be carried round about the fixed diameter KL and restored to the position from which it began to move; the figure so comprehended is a sphere whose diameter is KL (D11.14, D11.17). When the semicircle comes into the plane through KL and E, its circumference passes through E, because ME is equal to the radius MK (D1.15); in the same way it passes through F and through G. Thus the four vertices K, E, F, G of the pyramid lie on the surface of this sphere, and the pyramid is comprehended in it. Since KL = AB (Step 9), this sphere has its diameter equal to the diameter of the given sphere and is therefore equal to it; so the pyramid has been comprehended in the given sphere.

**Step 15.** The square on AB and the rectangle AB, AC stand under the same height AB, so the square on AB : the rectangle AB, AC = AB : AC (6.1). But the rectangle AB, AC is equal to the square on AD (Step 3), which is equal to the square on EF (Step 6). Therefore the square on AB : the square on EF = AB : AC.

**Step 16.** AB is triple of CB and AC is double of CB (Step 1), so AB exceeds AC by CB, which is the half of AC; that is, AB is one and a half times AC. Therefore the square on AB is one and a half times the square on EF. Since AB is the diameter of the sphere and EF is the side of the pyramid, the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid. Q.E.D.
